The dealfish, Trachipterus arcticus, is a rarely observed lampridiform of the northern Atlantic, whose life history parameters have largely been inferred from sporadic strandings and bycatch records. Field measurements of stranded adults indicate that this species attains a substantial ultimate fork length of 300 centimeters [Li = 300 centimeters], a dimension that places it among the larger members of the Trachipteridae. Analysis of the length-mass relationship from a modest collection of specimens suggests that an individual of this maximum length would correspond to an ultimate wet weight of approximately 38,800 grams [Wwi = approximately 38,800 grams], derived from a length-weight regression fitted to the available data. This pronounced body size, combined with its laterally compressed, ribbon-like morphology, distinguishes the dealfish from most other mesopelagic fishes in its range. The species is believed to occupy deep waters during the day and to undergo diel vertical migrations, which may occasionally bring individuals into shallower coastal zones where they become vulnerable to entanglement in fishing gear, providing the primary source of material for morphometric analyses.

Reproductive investment in the dealfish appears to be characterized by an exceptionally high fecundity, consistent with a pelagic spawning strategy. Under the cold, stable thermal conditions of its habitat, which remain near 5.2 °C [T = 5.2 °C], ripe females are estimated to release roughly 1,370 oocytes daily [Ri = roughly 1,370 oocytes daily], a remarkably high output that may represent an adaptation to compensate for elevated rates of egg predation in the open water column. The estimated wet weight at birth for this species is a mere 0.0031 grams [Wwb = 0.0031 grams], reflecting the small pelagic egg size typical of the group, which at just 1.8 millimeters in diameter gives rise to a lecithotrophic larva that depends entirely on a limited yolk reserve before the onset of exogenous feeding, a critical transition that likely imposes high initial mortality.

The timing of key developmental events in dealfish is closely linked to the cold, stable temperatures of their deep-sea environment. Gonadal maturation, marking the onset of puberty, is thought to occur at approximately 14 years after birth [tp = approximately 14 years after birth] when maintained at 5.2 °C [T = 5.2 °C], a protracted juvenile period that reflects the slow metabolic pace of life in cold waters. At this developmental milestone, a reproductively maturing individual would have attained a total fork length of roughly 200 centimeters [Lp = roughly 200 centimeters] at puberty. Applying the same allometric relationship, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is estimated to be 11,200 grams [Wwp = 11,200 grams], indicating that over half of the ultimate somatic growth is completed before reproductive tissues begin to mature. This pattern of delayed maturity is common in large, slowly growing ectothermic vertebrates that occupy food-limited environments and may prioritize the accumulation of sufficient body reserves to support the energy demands of a high-fecundity spawning event.

Longevity in the dealfish appears to be considerable, with a maximum lifespan estimated at 60 years [am = 60 years] based on extrapolations from growth increment analysis of vertebral bands, again under the cold thermal regime of 5.2 °C [T = 5.2 °C] that characterises its habitat. Such an extended lifespan is a predicted correlate of a slow life history, where delayed maturity and a large adult body size are traded off against a lower annual mortality rate, typical of many deep-dwelling teleosts that experience minimal predation pressure as adults. The combination of a 60-year lifespan and a protracted juvenile phase suggests that individuals have ample time to achieve growth to the maximum recorded dimensions before senescence begins to limit physiological performance. Age validation remains challenging for this species, however, as direct observation of wild individuals is extremely rare and mark-recapture studies have not been feasible, meaning that longevity estimates depend heavily on validated ageing techniques from a small number of specimens.

The observed reproductive strategy, which couples an extraordinarily high daily fecundity with a deferred age at first reproduction, may be interpreted as a bet-hedging adaptation to the unpredictable productivity of the mesopelagic environment. For a female reaching puberty at 14 years after birth [tp = 14 years after birth], the lifetime window for contributing to the next generation could span several decades, given the maximum recorded lifespan of 60 years [am = 60 years] at 5.2 °C [T = 5.2 °C]. During this reproductive phase, the sustained release of 1,370 oocytes daily [Ri = 1,370 oocytes daily] would result in a staggering cumulative output. This contrasts sharply with the minimal investment in each individual offspring, weighing only 0.0031 grams [Wwb = 0.0031 grams] at hatching, which underscores a classic r-selected component embedded within an otherwise K-selected life history framework. Comparative data from other lampridiforms, such as the closely related king-of-the-salmon (Trachipterus altivelis), would be valuable to determine whether this pattern is conserved within the family or unique to the extreme depths exploited by Trachipterus arcticus.
